title: Exploring Mars with Robot Rovers
summary: How robot rovers drive across Mars, take orders from faraway Earth, find signs of ancient water, and help people prepare to visit the red planet one day.
poll: Sending robots to explore Mars is better than sending people.

versions.title: Robots on Mars
versions.text:
Look at the sky at night. See the red dot? It is Mars. Mars is a planet, like Earth.

Mars is red. Its dust has rust in it. It is cold and dry. No one lives there.

Mars is far. A trip there takes months. So we send a robot. This robot has wheels. It is a rover.

A rover has eyes. They are cameras. It has an arm. The arm can drill a rock.

We send it a signal. The signal says where to go. But it is slow. It can take a long time. So the rover must think on its own.

Some rovers use the Sun for power. But dust can cover them. Some bring their own power.

One rover was to last 90 days. It went on for 15 years!

Rovers found rocks made in water. So Mars once had lakes. One rover now digs in an old lake. It took a small flying robot. It was the first to fly on a new world.

The UAE sent a craft, too. Its name is Hope. It looks at the air of Mars.

One day, we may go to Mars. Rovers help us get set.

versions.title: Robots on Mars
versions.text:
Look up at the night sky. You may spot a small red dot. That dot is Mars. It is a planet, just like Earth.

Mars is very far away. A trip there takes about seven months. So we send robots to look for us. A robot on wheels that drives on a planet is a rover.

A rover has cameras for eyes. It has a long arm with tools. The arm can drill a rock and test it.

People on Earth send the rover a signal. The signal tells it where to go. But it is slow. It can take up to 20 minutes to get there. So the rover must make some choices on its own.

Some rovers get power from the Sun. But red dust can cover them. Others bring their own power.

One rover was meant to last 90 days. It kept going for almost 15 years!

Rovers found rocks that were made in water. So long ago, Mars had lakes. One rover now works in an old lake bed. It took a small helicopter. It was the first to fly on a new planet.

The UAE sent a craft to Mars, too. It is called Hope. It looks at the weather on Mars.

One day, people may go to Mars. The rovers help us get ready.

versions.text:

One rover, called Opportunity, was meant to last 90 days. It kept going for almost 15 years!

One day, people may visit Mars. The rovers are helping us get ready.

versions.title: Exploring Mars with Robot Rovers
versions.text:
On a clear night, you might notice a small reddish dot in the sky. That dot is Mars, the fourth planet from the Sun. Mars is a lot like Earth in some ways, but it is very different in others.

Mars looks red because its dust contains rusty iron. The planet is cold, dry, and rocky, and its thin air would not let people breathe. Nobody can live there yet.

Mars is so far away that a spacecraft needs about seven months to reach it. Instead of sending people, scientists send robots. A robot that drives across a planet on wheels is called a rover. Each trip is part of a mission, a big plan with a goal.

A rover has cameras that act like eyes. It also has a long arm with tools. The arm can drill into a rock and take a sample, a small piece to test.

Engineers on Earth guide the rover with a radio signal. Because Mars is so distant, the signal can take up to 20 minutes to arrive. The rover cannot wait for every order, so it makes some choices by itself, such as steering around a large rock.

Some rovers get their power from the Sun, but red dust can pile up on them. Other rovers carry their own power supply.

A rover named Opportunity was built to work for 90 days. Amazingly, it kept going for almost 15 years!

Rovers have found evidence that Mars once had lakes and rivers. Some rocks formed in water. Today, a rover named Perseverance explores Jezero Crater, a huge round hole, that once held a lake. It also carried a small helicopter that became the first machine to fly on another planet.

The UAE sent its own probe, named Hope. It circles Mars and studies the planet's weather.

Someday, astronauts may travel to Mars. The rovers are helping them get ready.

versions.title: Exploring Mars with Robot Rovers
versions.text:
On a clear night, an observer might notice a small reddish point of light shining among the stars. That point is Mars, the fourth planet from the Sun. Although Mars resembles Earth in certain respects, it is a considerably more hostile world.

Mars appears red because its dust contains iron that has rusted. The planet is frigid, dry, and rocky, and its thin atmosphere contains almost no oxygen, so no person could survive there without specialized protective equipment.

Because Mars is so distant, a spacecraft requires about seven months to reach it. Rather than sending people, space agencies dispatch robotic explorers called rovers, which travel across the surface on wheels. Each rover carries cameras that function like eyes, as well as a robotic arm equipped with a scientific instrument for nearly every task, including a drill that can extract a sample from inside a rock.

Engineers on Earth direct every rover with radio signals. However, because the planets are so far apart, a signal can take up to 20 minutes to arrive. Since the rover cannot wait for every command, it is designed to be partly autonomous, meaning that it can make certain decisions independently, such as navigating around a hazardous boulder.

Some rovers rely on solar panels, although windblown dust can gradually coat them. Others carry their own long-lasting power supply.

One rover, Opportunity, was designed to operate for only 90 days. Remarkably, it continued exploring for almost 15 years.

Rovers have uncovered convincing evidence that water once flowed on Mars, because certain rocks contain layers of sediment, material that settles at the bottom of lakes and rivers. Scientists now wonder whether ancient Mars was habitable, meaning able to support tiny living things. Today, a rover named Perseverance is investigating Jezero Crater, an enormous depression that once contained a lake, and it seals rock samples in tubes for a future mission to return to Earth. It also transported a small helicopter called Ingenuity, which became the first machine to achieve powered flight on another planet.

The United Arab Emirates launched its own orbiter, named Hope, which circles Mars and studies the planet's weather.

Eventually, astronauts may journey to Mars, and the rovers are helping them prepare.

versions.title: Exploring Mars with Robot Rovers
versions.text:
Mars, the fourth planet from the Sun, appears reddish to observers on Earth because its surface is blanketed in iron-rich dust that has gradually oxidized over billions of years. Its atmosphere is thin, its climate frigid, and its surface arid, conditions that make the planet inhospitable to life as we currently know it but endlessly fascinating to scientists seeking to understand how such a world originally came to be. Reaching Mars is no small undertaking; a spacecraft must travel roughly seven months through interplanetary space before it can touch down on the Martian surface.

Once there, robotic rovers serve as scientists' eyes and hands, equipped with sophisticated cameras to document the terrain and a robotic arm fitted with a drill capable of extracting rock samples. Because the signal delay between Mars and Earth can stretch to twenty minutes, controllers cannot steer these vehicles in real time, and rovers are therefore designed to operate with a degree of autonomy, independently identifying and navigating around obstacles such as boulders without waiting for human instruction. Some rovers draw power from solar panels, while others carry their own internal power supply, a design choice that affects how far and how long they can travel.

The longevity of these missions has often defied expectations. Opportunity, for example, was originally engineered to function for only ninety days yet continued operating for nearly fifteen years, a testament to the durability of its design. Among the most compelling discoveries made by such rovers are distinct layers of sediment, geological evidence suggesting that liquid water once flowed across the Martian surface in its distant past.

The rover Perseverance currently explores Jezero Crater, a site specifically selected because its layered sediments hint at an ancient lakebed. As it investigates, Perseverance carefully seals promising rock samples inside specialized tubes, samples intended for eventual return to Earth for detailed laboratory analysis. The mission also carried a small helicopter named Ingenuity, which achieved the historic distinction of completing the first powered flight ever conducted on another planet.

Mars exploration is not the exclusive work of any single nation alone. The United Arab Emirates' Hope orbiter, for instance, studies the planet's weather patterns from orbit, contributing data that complements the ground-level findings of the rovers below. Together, these missions allow scientists to pursue one of the central questions driving Martian exploration: whether the planet, in some earlier chapter of its history, might once have been habitable.

Every instrument carried aboard a rover, from its cameras to its drill, must be engineered to withstand the mission's full duration without failure, since no technician on Earth can physically repair a malfunctioning instrument stranded millions of kilometers away on another planet's surface.

versions.title: Exploring Mars with Robot Rovers
versions.text:
Mars, designated the fourth planet in distance from the Sun, presents a distinctive reddish hue to observers on Earth, a coloration produced by iron-rich dust that has oxidized, or rusted, across billions of years of exposure. Its atmosphere is exceedingly thin, its climate persistently cold, and its surface characteristically dry, conditions that render the planet fundamentally inhospitable to life as it is understood on Earth, yet precisely these conditions have made Mars an object of sustained scientific fascination for those attempting to reconstruct its geological and climatic history. The journey itself demands considerable patience, as a spacecraft bound for Mars typically requires approximately seven months of transit before achieving a successful landing.

Upon arrival, robotic rovers function as extensions of scientific inquiry, outfitted with cameras capable of documenting the surrounding terrain in meticulous detail and a robotic arm equipped with a drill designed to extract rock samples for analysis. Given that the communication delay between Mars and Earth can extend to as long as twenty minutes, mission controllers are unable to direct these vehicles in real time, and rovers are consequently engineered to operate with substantial autonomy, independently identifying hazards such as boulders and recalculating their routes without awaiting explicit human instruction. While certain rovers rely upon solar panels for power, others are instead equipped with an internal power supply, a design distinction that meaningfully affects operational range and mission duration alike.

The operational longevity of these missions has, on numerous occasions, exceeded even optimistic projections. Opportunity, for instance, was originally engineered to function for a mere ninety days yet persisted in operation for nearly fifteen years, a remarkable testament to the robustness of its engineering. Among the most significant discoveries attributable to such rovers are stratified layers of sediment, geological evidence strongly suggesting that liquid water once flowed across the Martian surface during some earlier epoch of the planet's history.

Presently, the rover Perseverance continues its exploration of Jezero Crater, a location selected specifically because its layered sedimentary deposits imply the former presence of an ancient lakebed. In the course of this investigation, Perseverance seals promising rock specimens within specialized collection tubes, samples earmarked for eventual transport back to Earth, where they may undergo far more detailed laboratory analysis than is currently possible on the Martian surface itself. This mission additionally carried a diminutive helicopter named Ingenuity, which achieved the historically unprecedented feat of completing the first powered flight ever conducted on a planet other than Earth.

The exploration of Mars, moreover, is by no means confined to a single nation's efforts. The United Arab Emirates' Hope orbiter, as one notable example, examines the planet's atmospheric and weather patterns from orbit, generating data that meaningfully complements the ground-level findings gathered by rovers operating on the surface below. Taken collectively, these international missions enable scientists to pursue one of the most consequential questions underlying contemporary Martian exploration: whether the planet, during some earlier and markedly different chapter of its geological history, might once have been genuinely habitable.

Every scientific instrument carried aboard a rover, ranging from its imaging cameras to its sample-extracting drill, must be engineered with exceptional rigor to withstand the mission's entire anticipated duration without failure, since no technician situated on Earth can ever physically repair a malfunctioning instrument stranded millions of kilometers away upon another planet's unforgiving surface, a constraint that governs every design decision long before a rover ever leaves Earth.

keyWords.example: Engineers tested the new rover on sand dunes before sending it into space.

questions.stem: Which sentence best states the central idea of the article?
options: Mars is far too cold and dusty for any kind of machine to keep working there.
Robot rovers explore Mars for us and have taught us that water once flowed there.
The UAE was the very first country to land a spacecraft on the surface of Mars.
Rovers are controlled every second by people on Earth.
questions.why: The article explains how rovers work and what they discovered, especially about water.

wrong.A: Rovers work on Mars; one lasted almost 15 years.
wrong.C: Hope circles Mars; the article does not say the UAE landed first.
wrong.D: Rovers make some decisions by themselves.

questions.stem: How long does a spacecraft need to reach Mars?
options: About seven days
About seven years
About 20 minutes
About seven months
questions.why: The article says a spacecraft needs about seven months to reach Mars.

wrong.A: Seven days is far too short.
wrong.B: Seven years is far too long.
wrong.C: Twenty minutes is how long a radio signal can take.

questions.stem: What does the Hope probe do?
options: It drills deep into rocks.
It circles Mars and studies its weather.
It carries the first team of astronauts to Mars.
It flies like a helicopter.
questions.why: The article says Hope circles Mars and studies the planet's weather.

wrong.A: Rovers drill rocks; Hope stays above the planet.
wrong.C: No astronauts have gone to Mars yet.
wrong.D: Ingenuity was the helicopter.

questions.stem: The rover's arm can collect a sample. What is a sample?
options: A small piece taken to study
A message from Earth
A picture from a camera
A kind of wheel
questions.why: The article explains that a sample is a small piece the rover can test.

wrong.B: A message from Earth is a signal.
wrong.C: Pictures come from cameras but are not samples.
wrong.D: Wheels help the rover move.

questions.stem: Why do scientists send rovers to Mars instead of people for now?
options: People are not interested in seeing what Mars looks like up close.
Rovers travel much faster through space than any spacecraft can.
Mars is too harsh and far away for people right now.
Rovers can breathe the air on Mars.
questions.why: Mars is freezing, its air has almost no oxygen, and it is very far, so robots go first.

wrong.A: The article says people may travel there someday.
wrong.B: Rovers ride on spacecraft; they are not faster.
wrong.D: Robots do not breathe.

questions.stem: Why did scientists most likely choose Jezero Crater for Perseverance?
options: It is the warmest and sunniest place in the whole solar system.
It once held a lake, so it may hold clues about water.
It is the only flat and safe place to land anywhere on Mars.
It is close to Earth.
questions.why: The crater once held a lake, and scientists want to learn about Mars's watery past.

wrong.A: Mars is freezing; the article says nothing about a warm crater.
wrong.C: The article does not say this.
wrong.D: All of Mars is very far from Earth.

questions.stem: What can you infer about building a rover?
options: Engineers must plan for dust, distance, and long trips.
A broken rover can easily be fixed by the people who live on Mars.
Rovers never need power.
Any ordinary family car could drive on Mars without special tools.
questions.why: The article shows rovers must handle dust, slow signals, and a long journey, so engineers plan for these problems.

wrong.B: No people are on Mars to fix rovers.
wrong.C: Rovers need solar panels or their own power supply.
wrong.D: Rovers are special robots with tools and cameras.

questions.stem: How does the author organize the part about what rovers have found?
options: By telling a made-up story about an astronaut who visits Mars
By listing the steps for building a rover
By comparing Mars with the Moon
By giving a discovery and then the proof for it
questions.why: The author says water once flowed on Mars and then gives the proof: rocks that formed in water.

wrong.A: The article is nonfiction with no made-up astronaut.
wrong.B: It does not give building steps.

MID.prompt: Explain why rovers need to make some decisions by themselves. Use details from the article.
checklist: I explained the problem with signals from Earth.
I gave an example of a decision a rover makes.
I used at least two details from the article.
MID.modelAnswer: Rovers need to make some decisions by themselves because Mars is so distant that a radio signal from engineers on Earth can take up to 20 minutes to arrive, so the rover cannot simply wait for every instruction during its mission. For example, the article explains that a rover must steer around a boulder on its own rather than waiting for Earth to send a command, since by the time the signal arrived the rover could already be stuck.

keyWords.definition: able to act and make decisions without being controlled by someone
keyWords.example: The autonomous vacuum cleaner moves around the furniture by itself.

keyWords.definition: a tool used for careful scientific measuring or testing
keyWords.example: A thermometer is an instrument that measures temperature.

keyWords.definition: sand, mud, or small bits that settle at the bottom of water
keyWords.example: After the flood, a layer of sediment covered the road.

keyWords.definition: able to support life; good enough to live in
keyWords.example: The old house was repaired until it was habitable again.

keyWords.definition: a spacecraft that travels around a planet or moon without landing
keyWords.example: The orbiter took photos of the Moon's far side.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the central idea of the article?
options: Rovers are mainly useful for taking beautiful photographs of the Martian landscape to share with the public.
Robotic rovers overcome Mars's harsh conditions and distance to reveal its watery past and prepare for human exploration.
Mars was once covered by a huge ocean that still exists today in deep caves underground.
Scientists have already proved that many kinds of tiny living things exist on Mars today.
questions.why: The article covers how rovers cope with distance and harsh conditions, what they found about water, and how they help future astronauts.

wrong.A: Rovers also drill, test samples, and decide routes.
wrong.C: The article mentions ancient lakes and rivers, not a present ocean.
wrong.D: Scientists only ask whether ancient Mars was habitable.

questions.stem: According to the article, why is a rover designed to be partially autonomous?
options: Because radio signals can take up to 20 minutes to arrive
Because rovers are far too heavy for engineers on Earth to steer
Because Mars has no gravity to hold the rover on the ground
Because the engineers are asleep during the Martian day
questions.why: The delay in radio signals means the rover cannot wait for every command.

wrong.B: Weight is not given as a reason.
wrong.C: Mars does have gravity; the article does not say otherwise.
wrong.D: The article does not mention engineers' sleep.

questions.stem: What is Perseverance doing with the rock samples it collects?
options: Burning them as fuel to keep its instruments running at night
Throwing them away after taking a single photograph
Sealing them in tubes that a future mission may bring to Earth
Handing them up to the Hope orbiter for study
questions.why: The article says it seals samples in tubes that a future mission may return to Earth.

wrong.B: They are kept, not thrown away.
wrong.D: Hope circles Mars and does not collect rocks.

questions.stem: What made Ingenuity historic?
options: It was the first rover ever to drill into a Martian rock and test it.
It kept working on Mars for almost 15 years.
It was the first orbiter launched by an Arab country.
It was the first machine to achieve powered flight on another planet.
questions.why: The article says the small helicopter achieved the first powered flight on another planet.

wrong.A: Ingenuity was a helicopter, not a drilling rover.

questions.stem: In the article, the word habitable most nearly means —
options: covered in a thick layer of fine red dust
completely full of liquid water
able to support living things
located very far away from the Sun
questions.why: The text defines habitable as capable of supporting microscopic organisms.

wrong.A: Dust explains the color, not habitability.
wrong.B: Water is related, but habitable means able to support life.
wrong.D: Distance from the Sun is not the meaning.

questions.stem: Why would scientists want sediment layers in particular?
options: Sediment builds up in lakes and rivers, so it records Mars's watery past.
Sediment is the softest and easiest kind of rock for a rover to drill into.
Sediment protects the rovers from windblown dust and storms.
Sediment produces the oxygen that future astronauts will breathe.
questions.why: Sediment settles at the bottom of lakes and rivers, so layers of it are evidence of ancient water.

wrong.B: The article does not discuss how easy rocks are to drill.
wrong.D: The article does not say sediment makes oxygen.

questions.stem: Which comparison between power sources is supported by the article?
options: Solar panels never fail on Mars, but every other kind of power supply runs out within a few days.
Both kinds of power sources are completely blocked whenever dust blows.
Solar panels can be weakened by dust, while some rovers carry their own lasting supply.
Neither power source can work in the cold, thin air of Mars.
questions.why: The article says dust can coat solar panels and reduce power, whereas other rovers carry long-lasting supplies.

wrong.B: Only solar panels are described as affected by dust.
wrong.D: Both kinds have worked on Mars.

questions.stem: What can be inferred from the fact that Opportunity worked for almost 15 years?
options: Its engineers built it to be much tougher than its basic plan required.
Mars has no wind or dust storms.
Rovers do not need any power at all.
The rover was repaired by astronauts.
questions.why: Lasting far beyond its 90-day plan suggests the rover was very well built.

wrong.B: The article mentions windblown dust on Mars.
wrong.D: No astronauts have visited Mars.

HIGH.prompt: Should space agencies keep sending robots, or start sending people to Mars? Argue your position using evidence from the article.
checklist: I supported it with at least two facts from the article.
I explained one challenge that Mars presents.
HIGH.modelAnswer: I think space agencies should keep sending robots to Mars rather than sending people right now. The article shows how effective autonomous rovers can be, since Opportunity was only built to work for 90 days but instead kept exploring for almost 15 years, and the rover Perseverance has already found evidence that water once flowed in Jezero Crater. One major challenge that supports this position is Mars's harsh, unbreathable environment, since the article notes that its thin air would not let people breathe, which makes sending a robot a far safer way to gather evidence while rovers continue helping astronauts get ready for a future human mission.
